Run Monte Carlo sensitivity: assign distributions to weights (e.g., +/- 20% of nominal) and scores (e.g., +/- 1 point). Run 10,000 trials. Report the percentage of trials where each candidate wins. If the recommended alternative wins in more than 70% of trials, the decision is solid. Below 50%, the result is too close to call and additional data is needed.

Document the complete trade study. Future engineers will revisit this decision when requirements change. They need to understand not just what was decided but why, what alternatives were considered, and what would have to change for a different alternative to be preferred. Include dissenting opinions: if an evaluator disagreed with the recommendation, document their reasoning.

Write the decision record as a one-page summary for management and downstream teams who need to know the outcome without reading the full study. State the decision, the two strongest reasons supporting it, the main risk of the decision, and the trigger conditions that should cause the team to revisit it (e.g., if the cost of component X increases by more than 30%).

description: Plan and execute system verification and validation following the V-model, from test procedure development through execution to anomaly resolution, distinguishing between proving the build and proving the design.

steps.description: Create the verification plan mapping each requirement to its verification method, level, and event using the V-model structure.

inputs.name: requirements-set
inputs.desc: Complete set of system, subsystem, and component requirements with traceability

inputs.name: system-architecture
inputs.desc: Architecture showing test access points, built-in test capabilities, and integration sequence

outputs.name: verification-cross-reference-matrix
outputs.desc: Each requirement mapped to: verification method (test, analysis, inspection, demonstration), verification level (component, subsystem, system, operational), and the specific test or analysis that verifies it

outputs.name: test-architecture
outputs.desc: How the test environment is structured at each level: what is real hardware, what is simulated, what instrumentation is needed, and what the test environment fidelity is relative to the operational environment

outputs.name: verification-schedule
outputs.desc: When each verification event occurs in the program schedule, with predecessor dependencies (component tests complete before subsystem integration)

process: Assign a verification method to every requirement. Test: measure actual performance under controlled conditions. Analysis: calculate or simulate when testing is impractical or uneconomical (e.g., lifetime reliability, radiation hardness). Inspection: verify physical characteristics by examination (dimensions, labels, workmanship). Demonstration: operate the system and observe that it performs the required function (less rigorous than test, suitable for qualitative requirements).

Assign a verification level using the V-model. Component-level verification catches issues earliest and cheapest. Subsystem-level catches integration issues. System-level catches end-to-end issues. Operational-level catches environment and user-interaction issues. Verify at the lowest level possible: a voltage accuracy requirement is verified at the component bench, not at system integration.

Define the test environment fidelity at each level. At component bench, only the unit under test is real; everything else is test equipment. At subsystem integration, neighboring subsystems may be real or simulated. Document what is simulated and the fidelity of the simulation relative to the real system. Low-fidelity simulations can mask integration problems.

Build the verification schedule from the bottom up. Component tests complete before subsystem integration begins. Subsystem tests complete before system integration. System tests complete before operational testing. Include buffer time for anomaly investigation: historically, 20 to 30% of test time is consumed by anomaly resolution.

steps.description: Develop test procedures that are repeatable, measurable, and traceable to requirements, with explicit pass/fail criteria and measurement uncertainty accounted for.

outputs.name: test-procedures
outputs.desc: Step-by-step procedures for each verification event: setup, preconditions, step sequence, measurements, pass/fail criteria with tolerances, data recording requirements, and teardown

outputs.name: measurement-uncertainty-analysis
outputs.desc: For each quantitative measurement: instrument accuracy, calibration status, measurement technique uncertainty, and the test tolerance accounting for measurement uncertainty (guardband)

outputs.name: test-readiness-checklist
outputs.desc: Conditions that must be true before test execution: calibration current, test fixture verified, test article configuration confirmed, environmental conditions within limits, personnel qualified

process: Write each test step so that two different test engineers would execute it identically and obtain the same result within measurement uncertainty. Avoid ambiguous instructions like 'adjust until satisfactory.' Specify exact settings, wait times, measurement points, and acceptance thresholds.

Account for measurement uncertainty in pass/fail criteria. If the requirement is 'output voltage shall be 5.0V +/- 0.1V' and the measurement system has +/- 0.02V uncertainty, the test pass band should be 4.92V to 5.08V (guard-banded inward by the measurement uncertainty). This prevents accepting a product that might actually be out of specification.

Include acceptance criteria for the test itself (not just the product). The test is valid only if: environmental conditions were within specified ranges during the test, all instruments were within their calibration period, the test fixture was verified within its calibration interval, and no deviations from the procedure occurred. Invalid test results must be discarded and the test re-run.

Define the data package required from each test: raw measurements, calculated results, pass/fail status for each requirement, anomaly reports for any failures or deviations, environmental conditions during the test, and the configuration of the test article (serial number, hardware revision, software version). This package is the evidence that the requirement was verified.

steps.description: Execute verification tests, handle anomalies through structured investigation, and determine retest scope after anomaly resolution.

outputs.name: test-results
outputs.desc: Complete test data package with pass/fail status for each requirement, signed by the test engineer and witnessed by quality

outputs.name: anomaly-reports
outputs.desc: For each failure or anomaly: detailed description, conditions at time of occurrence, immediate containment action, root cause investigation results, corrective action, and retest plan

outputs.name: retest-scope
outputs.desc: After each anomaly resolution, the minimum set of tests that must be re-run to verify the fix without regressing other capabilities

process: Execute the test procedure step by step, recording all data in real time. Do not go back and fill in data from memory. If a step cannot be executed as written, stop and process a procedure deviation. Deviations may invalidate the test depending on their nature.

When a failure occurs, stop the test sequence and contain the anomaly. Record everything: what was measured, what was expected, the exact conditions (temperature, input stimulus, time into test), and any unusual observations (noise, smell, visual). Do not attempt to 'fix it and continue' without formal anomaly disposition.

Investigate the root cause using the 5-why method or fault tree analysis. The root cause must explain the observed failure completely. If the root cause is 'component X failed,' ask why it failed: was it overstressed, was it a manufacturing defect, was it a design margin issue? The corrective action must address the root cause, not the symptom.

Determine retest scope after the corrective action is implemented. If the fix changes only the failed function, retest only that function and any function that shares the changed hardware or software. If the fix changes a component that affects multiple functions (e.g., a power supply component), retest all functions that depend on that component. Err on the side of more retest rather than less.

steps.description: Validate the system by operating it in representative scenarios to confirm it meets the stakeholder needs, distinct from verification which confirms it meets the written requirements.

outputs.name: validation-results
outputs.desc: For each operational scenario: whether the system met the stakeholder's actual need (not just the written requirement), user feedback, and any gaps between what was specified and what was needed

outputs.name: requirements-gaps
outputs.desc: Requirements that were met (verified) but did not actually satisfy the need, and needs that have no corresponding requirement

outputs.name: acceptance-recommendation
outputs.desc: Recommendation to accept the system, accept with conditions, or reject, based on the combined verification and validation evidence

process: Distinguish validation from verification. Verification asks: 'Did we build the product right?' (does it meet the specification). Validation asks: 'Did we build the right product?' (does it meet the need). A product can pass every verification test and still fail validation if the requirements did not capture the real need.

Execute operational scenarios from the concept of operations. Use real or representative users in realistic environments. Observe how they interact with the system, not just whether the system performs to specification. Note workarounds, confusions, and unintended use patterns. These are validation findings even if no requirement is technically violated.

Identify requirements gaps: needs that were not captured in requirements (and therefore not verified) but are clearly important when the system is used in context. Also identify over-specified requirements: cases where the written requirement was stricter than necessary and drove unnecessary cost or complexity.

Compile the acceptance recommendation. Acceptance does not require zero deficiencies. It requires that all safety and mission-critical requirements are verified, all significant operational scenarios are validated, and any open deficiencies have an acceptable mitigation plan. Document the residual risks accepted by the decision authority.

description: Execute a system safety analysis from preliminary hazard identification through safety integrity level determination to safety case construction, supporting aerospace (ARP4761), automotive (ISO 26262), and industrial (IEC 61508) frameworks.

steps.description: Identify system-level hazards, assess their severity, and establish the safety requirements that the design must satisfy.

inputs.name: system-description
inputs.desc: Functional description and concept of operations

inputs.name: safety-standard
inputs.desc: Applicable safety standard: ARP4754A/ARP4761 (aerospace), ISO 26262 (automotive), IEC 61508 (general), DO-178C (software), or MIL-STD-882 (defense)

outputs.name: hazard-list
outputs.desc: Every identified hazard with description, causal factors, affected population, and severity classification per the applicable standard

outputs.name: safety-requirements
outputs.desc: Design requirements derived from each hazard: what the system must do (or must not do) to prevent or mitigate the hazard

outputs.name: hazard-tracking-log
outputs.desc: Living document tracking each hazard through analysis, mitigation, verification, and residual risk acceptance

process: Identify hazards by systematic methods: brainstorming with domain experts, checklist-based analysis from prior similar systems, HAZOP (deviation analysis: what if the output is too high, too low, absent, intermittent, untimely), and energy-based analysis (identify all energy sources that could cause harm if uncontrolled).

Classify each hazard severity per the applicable standard. ARP4761: Catastrophic (loss of aircraft), Hazardous (large reduction in safety margins), Major (significant reduction), Minor (nuisance), No Safety Effect. ISO 26262: S3 (life-threatening, survival uncertain), S2 (life-threatening, survival probable), S1 (light to moderate injuries), S0 (no injuries). IEC 61508: uses consequence categories tied to the specific application.

For each hazard, derive safety requirements. These are 'shall not' or 'shall limit' requirements: 'The system shall not produce output exceeding X under any single failure condition.' Safety requirements are non-negotiable and cannot be traded against performance or cost. They are verified with the same rigor as functional requirements but with additional independence (IV&V).

Establish the hazard tracking log as a living document. Each hazard entry includes: ID, description, severity, causal factors, safety requirements derived, design mitigations applied, verification evidence, residual risk, and acceptance authority. The log is reviewed at every design review and updated whenever the design changes.

steps.description: Determine the required safety integrity level for each safety function based on hazard severity, exposure, and controllability using the applicable standard's method.

outputs.name: safety-functions
outputs.desc: Each safety function defined: what it does, what hazard it mitigates, its required performance (response time, reliability), and its independence from the function it monitors

outputs.name: integrity-levels
outputs.desc: SIL (IEC 61508: SIL 1 to SIL 4), ASIL (ISO 26262: ASIL A to ASIL D), or DAL (ARP4754A: DAL A to DAL E) assigned to each safety function, with the derivation showing severity, exposure, and controllability inputs

outputs.name: target-failure-rates
outputs.desc: Maximum allowable dangerous failure rate for each safety function at its integrity level: SIL 1 = 1E-5 to 1E-6 per hour, SIL 2 = 1E-6 to 1E-7, SIL 3 = 1E-7 to 1E-8, SIL 4 = 1E-8 to 1E-9

process: Define safety functions: a safety function is a specific function that prevents or mitigates a hazard. It is not the entire system. 'Emergency braking' is a safety function. 'Brake system' is a subsystem that may contain multiple safety functions and non-safety functions.

For ISO 26262, determine ASIL using the three-factor method: Severity (S0-S3, from the PHA), Exposure (E1-E4: E1 = very low probability of operating scenario, E4 = high probability), and Controllability (C1-C3: C1 = simply controllable, C3 = difficult to control). The combination table yields ASIL A through D or QM (quality management, no safety integrity requirement).

For IEC 61508, determine SIL using risk graphs or LOPA (Layers of Protection Analysis). The risk graph considers consequence severity, frequency of exposure, avoidance possibility, and demand rate. LOPA is more quantitative: start with the unmitigated event frequency, subtract the risk reduction from each independent protection layer, and verify the residual risk meets the tolerable risk target.

Map the integrity level to design requirements. Higher SIL/ASIL requires: more rigorous development process (V-model at all levels), higher diagnostic coverage (the fraction of dangerous failures detected by self-test), architectural constraints (redundancy at SIL 3 and above), and independent assessment. The integrity level drives the engineering effort and must be determined early.

steps.description: Calculate the diagnostic coverage of the safety system's self-test mechanisms and verify that the architecture meets the target dangerous failure rate.

outputs.name: failure-mode-classification
outputs.desc: Each component failure mode classified as: safe (system goes to safe state), dangerous detected (self-test catches it), dangerous undetected (self-test misses it), or no effect

outputs.name: diagnostic-coverage-ratio
outputs.desc: DC = (dangerous detected) / (dangerous detected + dangerous undetected) for each safety function, compared against the SIL requirement (SIL 2 requires DC >= 60%, SIL 3 >= 90%)

outputs.name: proof-test-interval
outputs.desc: The required interval between comprehensive tests that can detect the dangerous undetected failures, calculated from the SIL target and the lambda_DU rate

process: Classify every failure mode of every component in the safety function. For each failure mode, determine: does it cause the safety function to fail dangerously (output wrong when needed)? If so, is the failure detected by any automatic diagnostic (watchdog, comparator, self-test, redundancy check)? If detected, it is dangerous detected (DD). If not, it is dangerous undetected (DU).

Calculate the diagnostic coverage ratio: DC = lambda_DD / (lambda_DD + lambda_DU). Compare against the architectural constraints from the standard. IEC 61508 Type A (simple) subsystem at SIL 2 with 1oo1D architecture requires DC >= 60%. SIL 3 with 1oo2D requires DC >= 90%. If DC is insufficient, add diagnostics or change the architecture.

For dangerous undetected failures, calculate the required proof test interval. The probability of failure on demand (PFD) for a single channel with proof test interval T is approximately PFD = lambda_DU * T / 2. For the system to meet SIL 2 (PFD < 1E-2), the proof test interval must be T < 2 * PFD_target / lambda_DU. If the required interval is shorter than operationally practical, add diagnostics to convert DU failures to DD.

Account for common cause failures between redundant channels. For a 1oo2 architecture, the PFD including common cause is PFD = beta * lambda_DU * T / 2 + (1-beta)^2 * (lambda_DU * T)^2 / 3. The common cause beta factor often dominates the PFD for high-SIL systems, meaning that adding more redundancy has diminishing returns without addressing common cause.

steps.description: Build the safety case as a structured argument that the system is acceptably safe, using goal structuring notation to link claims to evidence.

inputs.name: diagnostic-coverage-ratio
inputs.desc: DC calculations for all safety functions

outputs.name: safety-case-structure
outputs.desc: Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) diagram: top goal (system is acceptably safe), sub-goals (each hazard mitigated to acceptable level), strategies (how sub-goals are argued), solutions (the evidence: test results, analyses, field data)

outputs.name: evidence-index
outputs.desc: Every piece of evidence referenced in the safety case: test reports, analysis reports, design documents, process certifications, field data, with location and revision

outputs.name: residual-risk-register
outputs.desc: Every residual risk after mitigation, with its probability and severity, the risk acceptance rationale, and the authority that accepted it

process: Define the top claim: 'System X is acceptably safe for its intended use in environment Y.' This is the goal the entire safety case must support. 'Acceptably safe' means residual risk is below the tolerable risk threshold defined by the applicable standard or regulations.

Decompose the top claim using strategies. Strategy 1: argue over each identified hazard (show that each hazard is mitigated to an acceptable level). Strategy 2: argue over the development process (show that the process was rigorous enough for the integrity level). Strategy 3: argue over operational constraints (show that the operational procedures maintain safety). Each strategy decomposes into sub-goals.

Link each leaf-level goal to evidence. A claim like 'braking force meets the minimum threshold under single-fault conditions' must be supported by: the test report showing the measured braking force during the single-fault test, the test procedure traceability to the requirement, and the fault injection method used. Evidence must be objective and reproducible.

Identify and document assumptions and limitations. The safety case is valid under the stated assumptions (operating environment, maintenance schedule, user training). If any assumption is violated, the safety argument may not hold. List every assumption explicitly and assign monitoring responsibility to ensure they remain valid in operation.

steps.description: Apply systematic techniques to prevent common cause failures from defeating redundancy in safety-critical architectures.

outputs.name: independence-analysis
outputs.desc: For each redundant pair: physical separation, electrical isolation, software diversity, manufacturing lot diversity, and maintenance staggering assessment

outputs.name: common-cause-defense-score
outputs.desc: Scoring against IEC 61508 Annex D or equivalent: separation/segregation, diversity, complexity, assessment, competence, environmental testing, and environmental control, with an overall beta factor estimate

outputs.name: updated-residual-risks
outputs.desc: Residual risk register updated with common cause mitigation evidence and revised PFD calculations

process: Assess physical independence: are redundant channels in separate enclosures, on separate boards, powered from separate sources, routed through separate connectors? Physical proximity is the most common source of common cause: a single overvoltage event, a single thermal excursion, or a single mechanical impact can defeat both channels simultaneously.

Assess design diversity: are redundant channels implemented with different hardware (different IC families, different sensor technologies), different software (different algorithms, different compilers, different operating systems), and different design teams? Full diversity is expensive but dramatically reduces beta. Partial diversity (same hardware, different software) provides moderate common cause reduction.

Score the common cause defenses against IEC 61508 Annex D scoring system. Each defense category (separation, diversity, complexity management, assessment, competence, environmental testing, environmental control) receives a score from 0 to 3. The total score maps to a beta factor: score 165+ gives beta = 0.5%, score 130-165 gives beta = 1%, lower scores give higher beta values.

Recalculate the PFD with the revised beta factor and verify the safety integrity target is still met. If not, the options are: add diversity (expensive but effective), add diagnostics to detect common cause conditions before they propagate (moderate cost), or add a third channel to provide voting (expensive and complex). Document the chosen approach and its justification in the safety case.
